title: What He left unsaid
hook: Allah set duties and limits, and kept silent on things out of mercy, not forgetfulness, so don't dig into them
tomorrow: want to be loved? tomorrow's hadith says: want less. wait, what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the head, the pillar and the peak, and the small thing that holds the building: guard the tongue. Today, a hadith about what wasn't said at all.

Some rulebooks try to cover everything. Every case spelled out, and somehow each new rule breeds two more questions. Yesterday ended on a puzzle: how can leaving something unsaid be mercy? Hadith thirty, reported by Abu Tha'labah, has an odd phrase in it. Allah has set duties, so don't neglect them; set limits, so don't cross them; forbidden things, so don't violate them; and kept silent about other things, out of mercy for you, not out of forgetting. Not out of forgetting. Why would anyone need to be told that?
screen: `A RULE FOR EVERYTHING.` → `DUTIES, LIMITS, THE FORBIDDEN.` → `NOT OUT OF FORGETTING.`

segments.voice: Because a careful mind treats every silence as a gap. If the text didn't mention it, surely someone missed something, so let's dig until we find a rule. The hadith closes that door: the silence is on purpose, and it's a gift. That's the solve. The open space is part of the plan. Then the last line: so don't go digging into them. Sahih Muslim has a scene that shows why. The Prophet, peace be upon him, tells the people that hajj, the pilgrimage, has been made a duty. A man asks: every year? The Prophet stays silent. The man asks again, and again, three times. Then the Prophet says, in paraphrase: if I had said yes, it would have become a duty, and you couldn't have done it. Leave me be as long as I leave you be. The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's words: "Ask not of things which, if they were made known unto you, would trouble you." Jurists drew a principle from texts like these: in ordinary things, the starting point is that they're allowed. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: the silence isn't a hole in the law. It's room to live in, left there on purpose.
screen: `A SILENCE LOOKS LIKE A GAP.` · `THE SILENCE IS ON PURPOSE.` · `EVERY YEAR? THREE TIMES.` · `ROOM TO LIVE IN.` · then, large: `SILENCE IS MERCY TOO.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write by hand one question you keep circling, the one you've asked yourself five different ways. Underneath it, write: this one can rest. For the sit, keep your hand flat on the paper and let the question stay open, unanswered, without poking at it.
screen: `ONE QUESTION YOU KEEP CIRCLING.` · `THIS ONE CAN REST.`

segments.voice: What He left unsaid: the things Allah kept silent about, not forgotten, but left open as a mercy, so nobody has to dig them up.
For the road: silence is mercy too, and open space can be a gift. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1458 COUNTS.` → `HADITH 30 OF 42 · YEAR FIVE, 32 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: WANT TO BE LOVED? WANT LESS. WAIT, WHAT?`

howItsDone: Muslim jurists distinguish what the texts require, what they forbid, and what they leave open; in everyday matters, the common starting point is that a thing is allowed unless a text says otherwise.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3), puzzle shape: the odd phrase 'not out of forgetting' is the puzzle; the solve is that the silence is deliberate. Confirm the paraphrase of the hadith's four parts.

Sahih Muslim 1337: the man asks 'every year?' three times; the Prophet's answer paraphrased. The hadith's further line about earlier peoples ruined by many questions is deliberately left out so no tradition is a foil. Confirm the paraphrase and the number.
Qur'an 5:101 quoted from Pickthall 1930: confirm exact wording.

The principle 'in ordinary things the starting point is permission' (al-asl fi al-ashya' al-ibahah) is presented as something jurists drew from such texts; it is widely held but not universal in every domain (worship is treated differently). Confirm the framing.
Grading: al-Nawawi calls this hadith hasan (al-Daraqutni and others); some later scholars discuss a break in its chain. Only the trapdoor mentions grading.
